{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-vt-class-std","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"cba33e5de58234807ab469024d5c3c7e0e0b44ad9e058995613b4c3dd3334ed7","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-vt-class-std:lineage:19","source_registry_sha256":"0441bafe0dc257fd56d6bd0cd9054ad2b95889f94f5d3e5e6f98fb890bf902c4","source_liveness_sha256":"13f90fd88bb623234ea3628f2ee40ced3511148c14c82097743066ee414dd040"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Police stops, move over law, traffic signals and basic sign shapes","heading":"C — Police stops, move over law, traffic signals and basic sign shapes","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Police stops, move over law, traffic signals and basic sign shapes

FACT_ID: sec05-F01 | anchor: A01
Police vehicles signal a driver to stop by turning on flashing lights, or flashing lights together with a siren, and the driver should move as close as safely possible to the right side of the road without stopping in an intersection or pulling into the center median of a divided highway [A01].
Why it matters: Stop on the right, never in an intersection or the median.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F02 | anchor: A01
During a police stop keep your safety belt fastened until the officer has seen you wearing it, limit your own movements and those of passengers, breathe deeply and stay calm while the officer explains the reason for the stop [A01].
Why it matters: The belt stays on until the officer sees it.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F03 | anchor: A01
When the officer asks, show your license, vehicle registration and proof of insurance, stay in the vehicle unless asked to get out, and in a dimly lit area turn on the interior lights after stopping and before the officer approaches [A01].
Why it matters: Interior lights on in the dark protect both parties.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F04 | anchor: A01
The roadside is not the place to argue a traffic offense; the time to address it is in court [A01].
Why it matters: A frequently tested conduct rule.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F05 | anchor: A02
When a vehicle with flashing blue or red lights or a sounding siren approaches from any direction, the law requires you to pull over to the right side of the road, stop, and stay stopped until the emergency or law enforcement vehicle has passed [A02].
Why it matters: Any direction, pull right and stop until it has gone by.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F06 | anchor: A02
When you come upon a stopped police car showing flashing blue lights or a stopped emergency vehicle showing flashing red lights you must slow down and proceed with caution, and on a four lane road like an interstate you must also move over a lane whenever that can be done safely [A02].
Why it matters: Slow down everywhere, change lanes on four lane roads.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F07 | anchor: A02
A maintenance vehicle of the state, a city or a town that is working on a highway has the right-of-way, so a driver coming up on a snowplow with its lights flashing must slow with caution and give way to it [A02].
Why it matters: Snowplows get the same yield as emergency vehicles.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F08 | anchor: A02
Towing and repair vehicles usually show amber flashing lights, and a driver must use the same caution and procedures around these stopped vehicles as around stopped police and emergency vehicles [A02].
Why it matters: Amber lights earn the same slow down and move over response.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F09 | anchor: A02
Traffic signals control the right-of-way for smooth, orderly traffic flow, a dark signal such as one in a power failure is treated as a stop sign in every direction, and a signal that is out of order and flashing yellow or red must be obeyed as a flashing signal [A02].
Why it matters: A dark signal becomes an all way stop.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F10 | anchor: A02
At a red light stop before the stop line or the crosswalk, whichever comes first, and wait for green, although a green arrow that comes on during the red allows travel in the arrow's direction [A02].
Why it matters: Stop line first, then crosswalk.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F11 | anchor: A02
A right turn at a circular red light is usually allowed only after a complete stop, a scan of the intersection and yielding to pedestrians and other vehicles, and some intersections post signs or symbols forbidding a right turn on red [A02].
Why it matters: Right on red needs a full stop and no prohibiting sign.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F12 | anchor: A02
A police officer may direct you through a red light, and you should follow the officer's directions with caution [A02].
Why it matters: An officer overrides the signal.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F13 | anchor: A02
A yellow light warns that the signal is about to turn red, and a driver who is too close to the intersection to stop safely should proceed through with caution [A02].
Why it matters: Yellow means prepare to stop, not speed up.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F14 | anchor: A02
A green light allows you to proceed when it is safe, but a driver turning left must still yield to oncoming vehicles, and where extra emphasis is needed a left turn yield on green sign hangs from the overhead wire near the signal [A02].
Why it matters: Green never gives a left turner priority over oncoming traffic.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F15 | anchor: A03
A flashing circular red light is treated exactly like a stop sign: come to a stop, give way to every pedestrian, bicyclist and vehicle, and then go [A03].
Why it matters: Flashing red equals stop sign.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F16 | anchor: A03
A flashing yellow light means slow down, scan the intersection, yield to any oncoming vehicles before attempting a left turn, and proceed with caution [A03].
Why it matters: Flashing yellow means caution, not stop.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F17 | anchor: A03
A solid red arrow means drivers intending to turn left must stop and wait, and must not enter the intersection to turn while it is displayed [A03].
Why it matters: No left turn at all on a solid red arrow.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F18 | anchor: A03
A solid yellow arrow means the left turn signal is about to change to red, so drivers should prepare to stop, or prepare to complete the left turn if they are already legally within the intersection and no conflicting traffic is present [A03].
Why it matters: Already inside the intersection, you may finish the turn.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F19 | anchor: A03
A flashing yellow arrow lets drivers turn left only after yielding to all oncoming traffic, which has a green light, and to any pedestrians in the crosswalk, waiting for a safe gap before turning [A03].
Why it matters: Flashing yellow arrow is a permissive, yielding left turn.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F20 | anchor: A03
A solid green arrow gives left turns the right-of-way because the oncoming traffic is facing a red light [A03].
Why it matters: The protected left turn.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F21 | anchor: A03
A road sign's meaning can be told from its shape and color as well as its wording, so a sign covered by dirt or snow can still be read as regulatory, warning or information from its shape alone [A03].
Why it matters: Shape carries meaning even when the face is hidden.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F22 | anchor: A03
A stop sign has eight sides; at it you come to a full stop ahead of the stop line, the marked or unmarked crosswalk or the cross road, whichever is reached first, then scan the intersection, give way as required and proceed [A03].
Why it matters: Eight sides and a three point stopping rule.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F23 | anchor: A03
A yield right-of-way sign is shaped like an upside down triangle and means slow down, search, and enter only when the way is clear of pedestrians, bicyclists and vehicles [A03].
Why it matters: The inverted triangle is the yield shape.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F24 | anchor: A03
A circular sign bearing a large X and the letters RR warns that a railroad crossing is ahead [A03].
Why it matters: The round railroad advance warning sign.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0033]

Misconceptions:
- A yellow light means speed up to beat the red: false, it warns of the coming red, and only a driver too close to stop safely continues through with caution.
- A green light gives a left turning driver priority: false, the left turner yields to oncoming vehicles unless a solid green arrow is showing.
- Right on red is automatic: false, it requires a complete stop, a scan, yielding to pedestrians and vehicles, and no sign forbidding it.
- Only police and ambulances trigger the move over duty: false, maintenance vehicles like snowplows must be yielded to and amber lit tow trucks get the same caution.
- When police stop you, step out to speak with the officer: false, stay in the vehicle unless asked to get out.

Mnemonics:
- Eight sides stop, three sides yield, round for rails: the three basic sign shapes.
- Solid green goes, flashing yellow yields, red arrow rests: the three left turn arrows.
- Dark means stop sign all around: a signal with no lights is a four way stop.

Glossary:
- Move over law: the requirement to pull right and stop for approaching emergency vehicles and to slow down, and on four lane roads change lanes, for stopped emergency, police, maintenance or towing vehicles
- Flashing yellow arrow: a left turn signal that permits the turn only after yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians
- Protected left turn: a left turn made on a solid green arrow while oncoming traffic faces a red light
- Stop line: the painted line before an intersection where a driver facing a red light or stop sign must stop, ahead of the crosswalk
